blocks.eyebrow: Signs you are using too much
blocks.heading: Stinging, redness, light flaking — while following every instruction correctly
quotes: “Serum, toner, essence, masks. The more complete the routine, the more it stings.”
“All good products, all used together, and my face went red with no way to tell which one.”
“Retinol made me flake. I was told to push through, so I did.”
“A week off everything and my skin calmed right down — but the marks came back darker.”

explainer.heading: With a damaged barrier, every active behind it is beside the point
body: The outermost layer keeps water in and irritants out. When it weakens, actives penetrate faster than intended — which is why the same product can feel fine one week and sting the next.
This phase needs fewer things acting on the skin, not more. The four groups printed on this jar are all hydrating and soothing; there are no brightening or exfoliating actives in it.
It is a basic moisturising step. We call it that rather than a treatment, because putting treatment expectations on a moisturiser is the fastest way to be disappointed by one.

blocks.heading: Four steps through a phase when skin needs calm — this jar is the third
blocks.intro: A base moisturiser neither starts nor ends this phase. It keeps skin steady once you have dropped whatever was making it sting.

items.label: Signs of too much
items.body: Stinging, redness and light flaking even though you follow the instructions. The barrier is weak, so actives get in faster than intended.

items.label: Cut back the steps
items.body: Pause retinol, exfoliating acids and high-strength vitamin C. This phase needs fewer things acting on the skin, not more.

items.label: Base moisturiser, morning and night
items.body: This is where the jar sits: the last step of the routine, hydrating and soothing, with sunscreen added in the morning.

items.label: Back to actives
items.body: Actives come back once skin has settled again, not while it is recovering. This jar can stay on as your everyday moisturiser.

blocks.footnote: How long each step takes varies from person to person. If skin still stings, stays red or flakes heavily after you have cut back, that is no longer a moisturiser’s job — see a dermatologist.

blocks.eyebrow: Look at the photos, then at your own skin
blocks.heading: Which phase of skin this jar is for
blocks.intro: A basic moisturiser cannot do an active’s job. We go through each case so you do not buy the wrong expectation.

items.label: Red and stinging after too many actives

image.alt: Close-up of a flushed cheek on easily irritated skin

items.body: Red, stinging and lightly flaking even though you follow the instructions. Pause the strong actives, keep the routine short, and use this jar as the last step, morning and night.
items.fitNote: Exactly the phase this jar is for

items.label: Just stopped retinol or exfoliating acids

image.alt: Close-up of thin, sensitive skin with slight redness

items.body: During the break, skin is thinner and more reactive than usual. The four groups printed on the jar are all hydrating and soothing, with no strong actives added.

items.label: Dry and short of moisture all year

image.alt: Close-up of dehydrated skin with visible pores

items.body: No pigmentation concerns, just a frequent tight, dry feeling. Fine as a long-term daily moisturiser; while your skin is settled there is no need for a busier formula.

items.label: Just had a cosmetic procedure

image.alt: Close-up of reddened skin after a cosmetic procedure

items.body: This is the phase the jar is aimed at, but freshly treated skin is a clinical situation: ask the practitioner who did the procedure before you apply anything.

items.label: Wanting to fade melasma or dark marks

image.alt: Close-up of a light-brown melasma patch on the cheekbone

items.body: There are no brightening actives here. It keeps skin settled so other steps can work, but on its own it does not act on pigment — you need a different product.

items.label: Broken, weeping or persistently sore skin
items.body: Open, weeping or burnt skin is not the place for a moisturiser. If you have cut back on actives and skin still stings, stays red or flakes heavily, see a dermatologist.

blocks.caption: Close-ups illustrating each skin condition (brand image material), not before-and-after photos of the product in use. Not sure which phase your skin is in? Send us a photo and an adviser will take a look before you order.

blocks.eyebrow: Where it sits in the day
blocks.heading: The last step, morning and night
blocks.intro: While skin needs quiet, a shorter routine is better. This is the minimum.

steps.label: Rinse with cool water
steps.note: During this phase you can skip the morning cleanser.

steps.label: Collagen Peptide Cream
steps.note: Apply while skin is still slightly damp to hold that water in.

steps.label: Sunscreen
steps.note: Weakened skin darkens more easily after every exposure.

steps.label: Pause the strong actives
steps.note: Retinol, exfoliating acids, high-strength vitamin C — stop until the stinging ends.

steps.label: Collagen Peptide Cream
steps.note: A slightly thicker layer than the morning.

blocks.footnote: Most skin settles within one to two weeks once actives are reduced. If it is still stinging, red or flaking after two weeks, that is no longer a moisturiser's job — see a dermatologist.

items.q: How is it different from Smart Brightening Cream?
items.a: Different purpose entirely. The brightening cream carries pigment-targeting actives; this one is a base moisturiser that hydrates and calms. Use this when skin needs a rest, the other when you are running a pigmentation routine.

items.q: Can I use both at once?
items.a: Layering two moisturisers is not advisable. Pick one, according to the phase your skin is in.
Somewhere dry and cool, away from direct sunlight and heat. Close the lid tightly after use.
